macro_analysis.headline: Hot September PPI upends the disinflation story as hike odds climb; negative gamma, blowing-out credit, and a stressed MOVE leave equities exposed
macro_analysis.html:
Executive Summary

The morning opens with a macro development that changes the conversation. Overnight headlines report that U.S. September producer prices jumped at their fastest rate in more than four years, with one wire putting the print at 6.3% against expectations of 5.3%. That figure sits far above the 1.8% year over year September PPI in our stored series, and if the official number confirms it, the wholesale pipeline is re-pressurizing just as the bond market had settled into the disinflation trade. Fed funds futures have already taken the hint: this morning's snapshot prices a 33.2% chance of a hike at the October 28 FOMC and a 62.2% chance the target range reaches 4.00 to 4.25% by the December meeting, with further tightening priced through 2027. Fed's Mary Daly leaned into the narrative this morning, saying more rate hikes are likely, though not urgent in October.

Positioning looks fragile into that repricing. Dealer gamma in both index products is negative this morning, credit spreads are blowing out (the z-score spread minus VIX sits at 2.34, squarely in the blowing-out tier), and the MOVE index at 99.06 is pricing genuine two-sigma stress in rates vol while the VIX at 16.87 still reflects equity complacency. Bond vol and credit are telling one story, equity vol another. In our experience, that divergence resolves in favor of the fixed-income read more often than not.

Macro: The PPI Shock, Resilient Labor, Gasoline-Flattered Retail

The hot print. The single most important data point this morning is September PPI. Multiple wires this morning describe the September print as the biggest jump in more than four years, with expectations of 5.3% apparently beaten to the upside (6.3% per one headline). Our stored series carries September PPI at 1.8% year over year, itself up a tenth from August's 1.7%, so the series needs a hard refresh once the official release lands. The prior narrative was clean: PPI peaked at 2.6% in June and decelerated for three straight months, the textbook pipeline transmission from wholesale to consumer prices (September CPI at 2.4%). A September re-acceleration to multi-year highs would flip that story. It would argue the pipeline is re-pressurizing, whether through energy passthrough, diesel embedded in freight costs, or services costs that never fully cleared. Watch whether the bond desk treats this as noise or signal over the next 48 hours.

Labor is still not the constraint. Initial jobless claims printed 199,000 versus 200,000 expected, still below the 200,000 line and at historically low levels per the morning wires. Layoffs remain low. The picture is the same as all year: the labor market has not broken, which keeps the Fed's reaction function tilted toward the inflation mandate rather than the employment mandate. With CPI at 2.4% and PPI apparently re-accelerating, the Fed has neither a weak-labor reason to ease nor a soft-inflation reason to cut. That is the setup that puts hikes back on the table.

Retail sales beat, but read the mix. September retail sales reportedly rose 0.8%, beating forecasts, but spending excluding gasoline barely grew, and one wire explicitly attributes the beat to higher gasoline prices. That is the energy drag we have been tracking in the macro panel: with gasoline at $4.86 a gallon and diesel at $6.33, the nominal retail number is being flattered by the very energy tax that eats real purchasing power. Nominal retail strength plus stagnant ex-gas spending is the signature of cost-push, not demand-pull, and it sits uncomfortably alongside the PPI headlines.

Energy and geopolitics. Overnight headlines report Houthi attacks on Saudi Aramco facilities and King Khalid airport, with Saudi Arabia saying it thwarted a missile strike near Medina. Crude prices slid despite the Strait of Hormuz shipping threats, a curious response that suggests the market is fading geopolitical risk premium on confidence in the supply buffer. The more structural energy story is diesel: the IEA now says the global diesel squeeze drags into 2027. At $6.33 a gallon domestic diesel, freight surcharges keep embedding into goods prices, which is exactly the channel that would show up in a hot PPI print. The pipeline mechanics we have been tracking for three months just got a second wind.

Rates: Fed Funds Futures Are Pricing the Hike Cycle Back In

Fed funds futures this morning (EFFR 3.88, target range 3.75 to 4.00%) describe a market repricing toward hikes, not cuts:

  • October 28 FOMC: 66.8% probability of holding at 3.75 to 4.00%, 33.2% probability of a 25bp hike to 4.00 to 4.25%. One-in-three odds of a hike two weeks out is a very live meeting by recent standards, and it is consistent with Daly's phrasing that hikes are likely but not urgent in October, which leaves October on the table rather than ruling it out.
  • December 9 FOMC: 62.2% probability the range is 4.00 to 4.25%, 28.7% that it is 4.25 to 4.50%, and only 9.1% that it stays at 3.75 to 4.00%. The modal view is that the Fed hikes by year end, with nearly a three-in-ten chance it hikes twice.
  • Into 2027: the modal outcome at the January meeting is 43.3% for 4.25 to 4.50%; by March it is 40.4% for the same range; by June the modal outcome shifts to 34.3% for 4.50 to 4.75%. This is a term structure that prices a sustained hiking cycle, not a single insurance move.

The desk mechanics matter here. The September CPI at 2.4% gave the market permission to price gradual easing a month ago. This morning's PPI headlines revoke that permission. The mechanical consequence is that the implied terminal rate keeps ratcheting higher, which flows straight through equity discount rates: with the 10Y pinned in the 5.2 to 5.3% zone and the Fed repricing hawkish, the cost of capital is not coming down. Equities priced on falling discount rates are the most exposed cohort today.

Gamma Positioning: Both Index Products in Negative Gamma

The options desk starts the day in a fragile structure. Dealer gamma exposure is negative across both index products this morning (snapshot 10:09 AM ET), which means market-maker hedging will amplify intraday moves rather than dampen them:

  • QQQ: spot 718.42, total GEX negative 1.4 (calls +1.34, puts negative 2.74). Zero gamma sits at 738.17, roughly 2.7% above spot. With spot below the zero-gamma line, dealers are short gamma and must sell into weakness and buy into strength, mechanically exaggerating the day's move. The put wall at 700 is the next support level to watch: put open interest concentrates heavily there (over 423,000 contracts at the 700 strike), and dealer selling accelerates into it. The call wall at 760 caps the upside into any squeeze.
  • SPY: spot 765.08, total GEX negative 1.74 (calls +2.32, puts negative 4.07). Zero gamma at 773.43, about 1.1% above spot. Spot is sitting almost exactly on the put wall at 765, which makes the morning tape a knife's edge: a push below 765 flips dealer hedging from supportive to accelerating, since puts written at the wall go deeper in the money and dealers must keep selling to stay delta neutral. The call wall at 800 marks the top of the near-term range.

Both products share the same regime: negative net gamma, put-heavy positioning, spot at or below zero gamma. The market-implied message is that the crowd spent the overnight session buying downside protection, consistent with the morning wires describing a deepening tech sell-off in Nasdaq futures and with the skew readings below. In negative gamma regimes, the open and the first hour matter disproportionately, because dealer hedging in the opening cross sets the day's momentum. A break of SPY 765 or QQQ 700 to the downside is the level where the structure itself starts doing the selling.

Per-Ticker Gamma: AXON and AVGO in Negative Gamma, META Positively Positioned

The single-name books this morning mirror the index structure with one notable exception:

  • AXON: spot 402.00, total GEX negative 1.26, zero gamma 423.61 above spot, call wall 425, put wall 400. Spot is pinned near the put wall at 400 with zero gamma 5.4% overhead. Same mechanics as the indices: downside accelerates below 400, while any rally into 423 to 425 faces dealer selling at the zero-gamma flip.
  • AVGO: spot 339.89, total GEX negative 38.74, zero gamma 354.17, call wall 370, put wall 340. Spot is essentially resting on the put wall at 340. This is the most negatively positioned of the three names and the most exposed to an accelerated move on a break of 340.
  • META: spot 728.70, total GEX positive 196.21, call wall 750, put wall 730. META is the exception: positive gamma means dealer hedging dampens moves, and spot sits comfortably above the put wall at 730. That matters into the October 21 earnings print, with Rosenblatt at Buy ($886 target) and Truist at Buy ($1,000 target) both published this morning. The gamma structure gives META a calmer tape into the number, though the $1.15 million insider sale flagged in this morning's SEC filing coverage is worth logging as a datapoint on executive conviction.

Volatility Skew: Elevated Fear, Stable but Steep

Skew readings this morning (29 days to expiry) confirm active downside hedging across both indices:

  • QQQ: skew 10.6 points (7% OTM put IV 27.0 versus 7% OTM call IV 16.4), regime labeled elevated fear, trend stable with no day-over-day change.
  • SPY: skew 10.1 points (put IV 20.8 versus call IV 10.7), same elevated fear label, stable.

A ten-plus point skew is the options market charging a steep premium for portfolio insurance. The put side at 27.0% IV on QQQ is where fear lives, while calls at 16.4% are cheap and unwanted. That is the standard defensive configuration: the crowd is not betting on rallies, it is buying the right to get out. The trend reading is stable, meaning this is entrenched hedging rather than a fresh panic bid, which fits the view that the hot PPI narrative was already leaking into positioning before the wires caught up. Per-ticker skew coverage spans 32 names this morning; check the individual ticker pages for the single-name fear gauges.

Credit vs Equity Vol: Blowing Out, and the MOVE Keeps Flashing Red

This is the section of the desk that should worry the most this morning. The credit-vol tracker (October 14 close) shows the SHY-HYG spread z-score at 1.98 against a VIX z-score of negative 0.36, for a divergence reading of 2.34. That is above the 2.0 threshold that marks the blowing-out tier: credit is pricing meaningful stress while equity vol sits below average. Credit leads equities, not the reverse, so when the spread-VIX divergence prints above 2.0, the right posture is to assume equity vol is the mispriced leg.

The rates-vol side tells the same story more loudly. The VIX-MOVE divergence for October 14 stands at 2.45: the VIX closed at 16.87 (z-score negative 0.37, below average) while the MOVE closed at 99.06 (z-score positive 2.08, two full standard deviations above its trailing average). The bond market is pricing real stress around the rate path; the equity market is pricing 16-handle complacency. With this morning's PPI headlines repricing the Fed hawkish, the MOVE's read looks like the honest one. When these two vols converge, history says it is usually the VIX catching up to the MOVE, not the reverse.

Breadth, Rotation, and the Small-Cap Canary

Breadth is improving off a weak base, but the structure is still narrow. October 14 breadth: the spread at negative 12.97 (improved from negative 14.13), advance-decline ratio 1.13 with 261 advancers against 231 decliners, 39.4% of stocks above their 50-day moving averages, 51.7% above their 200-day. New highs beat new lows 16 to 4 on the day, and the 10-day net flipped positive to plus 10, though the 21-day net remains negative at minus 133. This is a market where the index holds near highs (the S&P printed 7,811.54 at its 52-week high on October 9) while the median stock trails. Narrow leadership plus negative gamma is a combination that can turn quickly on a down day.

Theme rotation is defensive. The October 14 quadrant map: Energy leading (relative strength 9.05, momentum 3.85), which fits $95 WTI and the overnight Saudi headlines; Cybersecurity leading (5.24, 1.09); AI and Semiconductors improving from lagging (negative 3.13, positive 1.17), a constructive early turn; Consumer Internet weakening (0.95, negative 1.47); and nearly every other theme, from Nuclear and Power Grid to Crypto, Defense and Aerospace, Quantum, Fintech, Clean Energy, Consumer Discretionary, and Biotech, sitting in the lagging quadrant. Leadership concentrated in Energy and Cybersecurity is not a risk-on board. The AI semiconductor turn toward improving is the one bright spot and is worth watching for follow-through today, especially with the tech tape under pressure.

Small and mid caps are the canary, and it is coughing. The Russell 2000 sits 2.25% below its 200-day moving average and 11.04% below its 52-week high at 2,729.53; the S&P 400 midcap is 0.64% below its 200-day and 8.04% below its high at 3,611.25. Both indices trading below their 200-day averages is the textbook breadth warning: the marginal buyer is not showing up for riskier equity. In a hiking-cycle repricing, small caps are the most duration-sensitive equity cohort, so this positioning is the fundamental expression of the same view the MOVE is pricing.

Sentiment and Positioning: Defensive Bid, Contrarian Longs, Closed Jaw

RSI cyclicals versus defensives: the ratio RSI sits at 34.81, in oversold territory, with the ratio at 1.2956 below its 50-day moving average of 1.3616. Cyclicals have been sold hard relative to defensives, and the signal flags a defensive bid: money is hiding in staples, utilities, and healthcare rather than rotating into cyclicals. That is textbook late-cycle positioning, not early-recovery positioning, and it rhymes with the breadth narrowness.

AAII sentiment: the week ending October 7 shows bullish at 40.3% (up 5.7 points on the week), bearish at 39.0% (down 7.5), neutral 20.8%, for a bull-bear spread of positive 1.3. Bulls just retook the lead, which from a contrarian perspective is not the read one wants when credit is blowing out and gamma is negative. Retail optimism at this juncture is a mild contrarian negative, especially with institutional positioning already defensive.

COT positioning (October 6 report): commercial dealers net short 30.9% of open interest in S&P 500 futures, large speculators (leveraged funds) net short 21.3%, and small specs (the retail proxy) net long 5.7%. The same pattern holds in Nasdaq-100 futures: commercials negative 23.1%, large specs negative 9.0%, small specs positive 4.4%. Everyone with an institutional balance sheet is net short except retail, which is net long. That is classic contrarian fuel: if the market rallies, the shorts have to cover, but if the negative-gamma structure takes over to the downside, retail longs are the liquidity being sold into. Watch this week's COT update to see whether leveraged funds pressed shorts after the PPI headlines.

Alligator jaw: closed as of October 9, with the S&P at 7,811.54 printing a 52-week high and 4-week forward EPS revision momentum at positive 2.1% (forward 12-month EPS $408.98). Earnings estimates are still being revised up even as the jaw stays shut, which is the one genuinely bullish fundamental input on the desk this morning. The risk is that a hawkish Fed repricing starts cutting those estimate revisions, at which point the jaw opens and the 2000 and 2007 analog playbook becomes relevant.

What to Watch Today

  • The PPI follow-through: confirm the official September PPI number versus the morning headlines. If 6.3% is confirmed, the June 2.6% peak thesis is dead and the wholesale pipeline is re-pressurizing. Watch the 10Y for a break that validates it.
  • SPY 765 and QQQ 700: both indices sit on or near their put walls in negative gamma. Holds and bounces there are orderly; breaks accelerate.
  • The credit-equity catch-up: spread-VIX at 2.34 and MOVE-VIX at 2.45 both say equity vol is mispriced low. A VIX break above 20 on any follow-through selling is the convergence trade starting.
  • Small caps and AI semis: RUT below its 200-day is the canary; AI and Semiconductors rotating into the improving quadrant is the offset. Whichever side confirms today sets the tone for the week.
  • The data pipeline: the retail sales control group, October CPI, and the next payrolls print are the swing factors that decide whether the market is pricing a one-off PPI scare or a genuine re-acceleration.
